---
title: 'Logarithmic Spiral ($e^x$)'
format: html
code-fold: True
---

When a young fern sprout (known as a fiddlehead) is tightly coiled, it forms a logarithmic spiral.
Logarithmic spirals often appear in nature, such as in nautilus shells, hurricanes, and spiral galaxies.

![Logarithmic spiral in fiddlehead](figures/Spiral-Fiddlehead.jpeg){height="1.3in" fig-pos="H"}
![Logarithmic spiral in Nautilus Shell](figures/Spiral-Nautilus.png){height="1.3in" fig-pos="H"}
![Logarithmic spiral in Hurricane](figures/Spiral-Hurricane.jpg){height="1.3in" fig-pos="H"}
![Logarithmic spiral in Spiral Galaxies](figures/Spiral-Galaxies.jpg){height="1.3in" fig-pos="H"}

A special feature of a logarithmic spiral is that its shape always stays the same (it has complete self-similarity). If you shrink or enlarge the spiral by any amount, it is possible to rotate it so that it matches the original spiral.

![A logarithmic spiral is completely self-similar.](figures/Spiral-Self-Similarity.png){width="6in" fig-pos="H"}
